The Moon-Weaver spent her eons spinning the tides, weaving the currents into intricate lace to keep the seabed tidy. She was content, but she possessed one great weakness: she was a collector of sorrows. 

Whenever a mortal on the surface suffered a heartbreak, or a lost sailor wept for a home he would never see, or a mother mourned a child taken by the wind, their tears did not simply vanish into the earth. They trickled down through the porous rock, filtering through the sand, until they gathered in the velvet halls of the Moon-Weaver.

She believed that if she gathered every tear ever shed, she could eventually weave them into a great, shimmering cloak of empathy—a garment that, if worn by the world, would end all suffering.

For ten thousand years, she stored the salt-water of human grief in great crystal amphorae. But the heart of humanity is a bottomless well, and the sorrows grew too heavy for the glass to hold. One night, during a particularly cruel winter of war and famine, the weight of the world’s misery became an unbearable tide. 

The great amphorae shattered all at once.

The concentrated essence of a billion heartbreaks surged outward in a violent, white spray, flooding the sweet waters of the mirror-sea. The silver turned to turquoise, and the sweetness turned to brine.

The Moon-Weaver, devastated by the loss of her work, ascended to the sky, where she remains to this day. She still reaches down with her gravity, trying to pull the salt back toward her, tugging at the shores in a rhythmic, eternal longing. 

And that is why the sea is salty: it is the preserved memory of every tear the world has ever cried, held in the blue embrace of the deep.

They lived in a state of eternal longing, for they could never truly embrace. Whenever the Sky leaned down to kiss the waves, he brought the storms; whenever the Sea rose up to meet him, she brought the fog.

She kept these sorrows in a great, translucent urn, for she knew that if grief were left to wander the earth, it would poison the soil and wither the forests.

One eon, the Sky grew jealous of the land. He saw how the mountains could hold the earth and how the forests could cling to the hills. He wanted something to hold onto—something permanent. He begged the Weaver of Tears for a gift that would bind him to the Sea forever.

The Weaver, pitying the lonely Sky, agreed to help. But she had no gold or diamonds to give. She had only the urn of sorrows. 

"I can give you a bond," the Weaver whispered, "but it is a heavy one. It is the weight of every heartbreak, every lost love, and every silent goodbye ever felt by a creature of the earth."

The Sky, blinded by his longing, agreed. The Weaver tipped the great urn, pouring a cascading river of crystalline salt into the turquoise depths of the Sea.

The effect was instantaneous. The water grew heavy and dense, anchoring the Sea to the earth so she could no longer drift away. The salt acted as a cosmic glue, weaving the essence of the Sky’s longing into the very chemistry of the water. Now, whenever the Sky weeps in the form of rain, he is simply trying to wash away the bitterness of that ancient bargain.

And so the sea remains salty—not from anger or malice, but because it carries the weight of every tear ever shed, holding the ocean in a permanent, aching embrace with the horizon.

The Moon, though fond of the Ocean, was a wanderer of the void. She loved him, but she loved her freedom more. For eons, she danced just out of reach, her pale light teasing the surface of the water, promising a union that the laws of nature forbade.

One night, the Ocean could bear the distance no longer. But the gravity of the world is a jealous master. The Ocean was pulled back down with a violence that shook the seabed. As he crashed back into his basin, his heart—which had been pure, sweet water—shattered from the grief of the fall.
